_expect.name: Precipice aka The South Wall, The

me_precipice_aka_the_south_wall_the.blurb:
The South Wall is the main traditional cliff on Champlain Mountain in Acadia National Park, a broad face of glaciated pink granite reaching a little over two hundred feet at its tallest. Routes run one to three pitches up clean dihedrals, cracks and slabby faces on solid rock.

Grades span 5.3 to 5.12, with most lines from 5.9 to 5.11 and several long-standing moderate classics below that, so it suits confident trad leaders and parties stepping up to multi-pitch. A standard rack of nuts and small to medium cams covers most routes. It sits above the park's famous cliffside trail, and the views over Frenchman Bay are a big part of the draw.

co_quarry_wall_at_the_bank.blurb:
The Quarry Wall is a limestone face on the northern side of The Bank at Shelf Road, farther up the canyon than the main Bank walls and well left of Piggy Bank. It is mostly bolted sport climbing with a few trad lines and a little bouldering, on the pocketed, edgy rock Shelf Road is known for.

Lines are single pitch, from 5.6 to 5.11 with most at 5.10. It is a good pick for climbers who want a quieter corner than the busiest Bank sections, and for a mixed group wanting both moderate and harder sport leads.

co_castle_rock_2.blurb:
Castle Rock is the prominent granite outcrop at the Nederland end of Boulder Canyon, right beside the highway. It holds a wide mix of traditional lines from 5.5 to the 5.14s with most at 5.11 and 5.12, a few sport routes and aid lines, and boulder problems from V0 to V14; its position by the road makes it one of the easiest places in the canyon to reach.

The rock is Front Range granite with cracks, slabs and steeper faces, so it suits trad climbers across a range of abilities and anyone wanting a quick after-work lap.
co_castle_rock_2.approach: The base of the formation is a short flat step from the roadside pullout; the ground at the foot is uneven.

ut_cat_wall.blurb:
Cat Wall is a Wingate sandstone cliff in the northern part of Indian Creek, home to the straight-in splitter crack climbing the area is famous for. Routes are traditional single-pitch cracks from 5.10 to 5.13, the great majority at 5.11, with a handful of bolted lines, and many carry cat-themed names.

The cracks are sustained and parallel-sided, so success depends on carrying several cams of one size and on hand, fist and finger technique rather than face moves. It suits climbers who already lead trad and want to work on crack craft. The sandstone turns fragile when wet, so climbing after rain should wait.
ut_cat_wall.approach: Pass through the ranch gate from the turnout, shutting it behind you, and follow the trail northeast toward the wall. It is a long walk of nearly two miles across open desert.

tn_sunset_south.blurb:
The southern stretch of the Sunset Rock cliff line sits on the western brow of Lookout Mountain, high above Chattanooga. It is a traditional-protection venue with nearly a hundred routes, mostly cracks and corners from 5.4 to 5.13 with the bulk at 5.9 and 5.10, on a long, tree-shaded edge with open views over the valley.

The climbing is gear-oriented and no new bolts or pitons are added here, which keeps the character close to its older roots. It suits climbers comfortable placing their own protection who want short, accessible routes right next to town.
tn_sunset_south.parking_note: Drive up Lookout Mountain to West Brow Road at the rim, where the small lot holds only a handful of cars and has a short time limit. If it is full, park lower down at the climbers' lot or near the Cravens House rather than on the street.

nh_fire_tower_the.blurb:
The Fire Tower area lies on the slopes of South Mountain in Pawtuckaway State Park, among the boulder-strewn woods that make the park a well-known southern New Hampshire bouldering destination. Most of its roughly ninety problems are boulders from V0 to V10 with a deep middle at V3 to V5, plus a couple of trad lines, spread across scattered blocks and small walls beneath the trees.

The landings are typical of the park, rooty and uneven, so pads and spotters matter. It suits boulderers who like a shaded forest setting and a short, steady walk from the trail to the blocks.
nh_fire_tower_the.approach: Follow the Fire Tower Trail up South Mountain. About five minutes up, where the trail turns sharply right, a faint footpath leads left and downhill to a warm-up alcove formed by boulder walls, with more blocks nearby.

co_gym_the.blurb:
The Gym is a steep limestone wall at Shelf Road, north of the big hairpin on the road in, holding some of the hardest and most overhanging sport climbing in the area: lines from 5.10 to 5.13 with the bulk at 5.12. Nearly all of it is bolted, and the rock is brittle enough that the few trad lines are treated with caution.

Because it is a long walk beyond the busier cliffs, it stays quiet. It suits strong sport climbers after steep, powerful lines and space to themselves. A 60 m rope is preferred, though a 50 m reaches most routes.
co_gym_the.approach: From the day-use lot at The Bank, take the Cactus Cliff trail along the base of The Bank, past The Vault and Cactus Cliff, then along Spiney Ridge and north to The Gym — roughly fifteen minutes beyond the walk to Cactus.
